blocks.body:
How much paint covers a wall, how much water fills a tank, how much land is in a field? Area and volume answer these, and the formulas are familiar. Less familiar is why they are true: why a cone holds exactly a third of the cylinder around it, or why the surface of a ball is $4\pi r^2$.

This page builds the standard formulas from three ideas, cut-and-rearrange, cross-sections and scaling, using facts about triangles from [[euclid-basics]] and circles from [[circles]]. At the end we see how calculus computes areas and volumes, and why a fully precise notion of volume is subtler than it looks.

blocks.title: Area by cutting and rearranging
blocks.body:
Area is measured in unit squares, and an $a \times b$ rectangle holds $ab$ of them (exactly when $a, b$ are whole numbers, and by approximation in general). Two rules then do most of the work: congruent figures have equal area, and if a figure is cut into pieces, its area is the sum of their areas.

- Parallelogram: cut a right triangle off one end and slide it to the other; you get a rectangle with the same base $b$ and height $h$. Area $bh$.
- Triangle: two copies of a triangle fit together into a parallelogram, so its area is $\frac12 bh$. If two sides $a, b$ meet at angle $C$, the height onto $b$ is $a\sin C$, so the area is $\frac12 ab\sin C$.
- Trapezium with parallel sides $a, b$ and height $h$: two copies, one turned upside down, form a parallelogram with base $a + b$. Area $\frac12 (a+b)h$.

Every polygon can be cut into triangles, so these rules give the area of any polygon.

blocks.title: Circles and radians
blocks.body:
All circles are similar, so the ratio of circumference to diameter is the same for all of them; this constant is $\pi \approx 3.14159$. A circle of radius $r$ has circumference $2\pi r$.

For the area, cut the disc into many thin sectors like slices of a pizza and lay them side by side, alternately pointing up and down. The result is nearly a parallelogram whose height is $r$ and whose base is half the circumference, $\pi r$. As the slices get thinner the approximation becomes perfect, giving area $\pi r^2$.

An angle $\theta$ in radians is the arc length it cuts off on a circle of radius 1; a full turn is $2\pi$. On a circle of radius $r$, an angle $\theta$ at the centre cuts off an arc of length $r\theta$ and a sector of area $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\cdot \pi r^2 = \frac12 r^2\theta$. These formulas are the main reason radians are used: in degrees they carry an awkward factor $\frac{\pi}{180}$.

blocks.title: Scaling law
blocks.body: If a figure is enlarged by scale factor $k > 0$ (every length multiplied by $k$), its area is multiplied by $k^2$. If a solid is enlarged by scale factor $k$, its surface area is multiplied by $k^2$ and its volume by $k^3$.

blocks.title: Why
blocks.body: A unit square becomes a $k \times k$ square, of area $k^2$; a unit cube becomes a $k \times k \times k$ cube, of volume $k^3$. A rectangle or box built from such units scales the same way. A general shape can be approximated from inside and outside by unions of tiny squares (or cubes); enlarging the shape enlarges each tiny square, multiplying every approximation by $k^2$ (or $k^3$), so it multiplies the area (or volume) too. For triangles you can also see it directly: base and height both get multiplied by $k$, so $\frac12 bh$ gets multiplied by $k^2$.

blocks.title: Volume and Cavalieri's principle
blocks.body:
A box $a \times b \times c$ holds $abc$ unit cubes. A prism or cylinder is a base of area $A$ moved straight up through height $h$, and its volume is $Ah$: think of it as a stack of thin identical slices.

Now imagine a stack of coins. Push it so that it leans; its shape changes, but every coin is still there, so the volume does not change. This is the idea behind Cavalieri's principle: if two solids lie between the same two parallel planes, and every plane parallel to them cuts both solids in cross-sections of equal area, then the solids have equal volume. In particular a slanted prism or cylinder with base area $A$ and perpendicular height $h$ still has volume $Ah$. At school the principle is taken as a basic fact; with calculus it becomes the formula $V = \int A(z)\,dz$, where $A(z)$ is the area of the cross-section at height $z$.

blocks.title: Pyramids and cones
blocks.body: A pyramid or cone with base area $A$ and perpendicular height $h$ has volume $\frac13 Ah$. In particular a circular cone of radius $r$ has volume $\frac13\pi r^2 h$.

Step 1: a special pyramid. Take a cube of side $a$ and a vertex $O$ of it. The three faces of the cube not containing $O$ are bases of three square pyramids with apex $O$, each of height $a$, and these three pyramids are congruent and fill the cube. So each has volume $\frac13 a^3 = \frac13 (a^2)(a)$.

Step 2: any height. Stretching that pyramid vertically by a factor $\frac{h}{a}$ multiplies every horizontal slice's thickness, and hence the volume, by $\frac{h}{a}$. So a pyramid on an $a \times a$ square with its apex above a corner and height $h$ has volume $\frac13 a^2 h$.

Step 3: any base. Cut a pyramid or cone with base area $A$ and height $h$ by a plane parallel to the base at height $z$. The section is a copy of the base shrunk towards the apex by the factor $\frac{h - z}{h}$, so its area is $A\left(\frac{h-z}{h}\right)^2$ by the scaling law. This depends only on $A$, $h$ and $z$, not on the shape of the base or where the apex sits. By Cavalieri's principle, all pyramids and cones with base area $A$ and height $h$ have the same volume as the square pyramid of Step 2 with $a^2 = A$, which is $\frac13 Ah$.

With calculus the same cross-sections give it in one line: $\int_0^h A\left(1 - \frac{z}{h}\right)^2 dz = \frac13 Ah$.

blocks.title: The sphere (Archimedes)
blocks.body: A ball of radius $r$ has volume $\frac43 \pi r^3$ and its surface has area $4\pi r^2$.

Compare a hemisphere of radius $r$ with a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $r$ from which a cone has been removed: the cone has its base on the top of the cylinder and its apex at the centre of the bottom. Stand both on a table.

At height $z$ (with $0 \le z \le r$), the hemisphere's cross-section is a disc of radius $\sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$ by Pythagoras, so its area is $\pi(r^2 - z^2)$. The other solid's cross-section is a ring: the cylinder gives a disc of radius $r$, and the cone, whose radius grows from 0 at the bottom to $r$ at the top, removes a disc of radius $z$. Its area is $\pi r^2 - \pi z^2$. The areas agree at every height, so by Cavalieri's principle the volumes agree:
$$V_{\text{hemisphere}} = \pi r^2 \cdot r - \tfrac13 \pi r^2 \cdot r = \tfrac23 \pi r^3,$$
and the whole ball has volume $\frac43\pi r^3$.

For the surface, think of a thin shell between radii $r$ and $r + \delta$. Its volume is $$\frac43\pi (r+\delta)^3 - \frac43 \pi r^3 = 4\pi r^2 \delta + 4\pi r\delta^2 + \frac43\pi\delta^3$$, and it is also approximately (surface area) $\times\, \delta$. Dividing by $\delta$ and letting $\delta \to 0$ gives surface area $4\pi r^2$, the derivative of the volume.

blocks.title: Surfaces, calculus and what volume really is
blocks.body:
Other curved surfaces can be unrolled. A cylinder's side unrolls into a rectangle $2\pi r$ by $h$, area $2\pi rh$. A cone's side, with slant height $l$, unrolls into a sector of radius $l$ whose arc is $2\pi r$; a sector's area is half its radius times its arc, so the area is $\frac12 \cdot l \cdot 2\pi r = \pi rl$. A sphere cannot be unrolled flat without stretching, which is why we used the shell argument.

Calculus turns Cavalieri's principle into a general method; see [[integral-applications]]. Rotating the graph of $y = f(x)$, $a \le x \le b$, about the $x$-axis sweeps out a solid whose cross-sections are discs of area $\pi f(x)^2$, so its volume is $\pi\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx$. With $f(x) = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$ on $[-r, r]$ this gives $\pi\left[r^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-r}^{r} = \frac43\pi r^3$ again.

What is area, precisely? For polygons, the Wallace–Bolyai–Gerwien theorem says two polygons of equal area can always be cut into finitely many pieces that rearrange from one to the other. In space this fails: soon after Hilbert posed the question in 1900 as his third problem, Dehn proved that some polyhedra of equal volume cannot be cut into matching polyhedral pieces; a cube and a regular tetrahedron of the same volume are an example. So volume genuinely needs limits. For wild sets even limits are not enough: the Banach–Tarski paradox cuts a ball into five pieces that reassemble, by rotations and translations, into two balls of the original size. Those pieces cannot be assigned any volume, and [[lebesgue]] measure explains which sets do.

blocks.title: A segment of a circle
blocks.body: A chord cuts off an arc of a circle of radius 6 subtending an angle of $60^\circ$ at the centre. Find the area of the smaller region between the chord and the arc.
blocks.solution: In radians the angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. The sector has area $\frac12 \cdot 6^2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = 6\pi$. The triangle formed by the chord and the two radii has area $\frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 6 \cdot \sin 60^\circ = 9\sqrt3$. The segment is the difference: $6\pi - 9\sqrt3 \approx 3.26$.

blocks.title: The frustum
blocks.body: A lampshade is a cone with its top cut off by a plane parallel to the base: a frustum with base radius $R$, top radius $r < R$ and height $h$. Show that its volume is $\frac13\pi h(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$, and evaluate it for $R = 3$, $r = 1$, $h = 4$.
blocks.solution:
Complete the frustum to a cone of height $H$. The small cone that was cut off has height $H - h$ and is similar to the big one, so $\frac{r}{H - h} = \frac{R}{H}$. Solving, $H = \frac{hR}{R - r}$ and $H - h = \frac{hr}{R - r}$. The frustum's volume is
$$\frac13\pi R^2 H - \frac13 \pi r^2 (H - h) = \frac{\pi h}{3}\cdot\frac{R^3 - r^3}{R - r} = \frac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + Rr + r^2),$$
using $R^3 - r^3 = (R - r)(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$. For $R = 3$, $r = 1$, $h = 4$: $\frac{4\pi}{3}(9 + 3 + 1) = \frac{52\pi}{3}$.

Check the extremes: $r = R$ gives $\pi R^2 h$, a cylinder; $r = 0$ gives $\frac13\pi R^2 h$, a cone.

blocks.title: A tetrahedron inside a cube
blocks.body: Find the volume of a regular tetrahedron with edge $a$, without using any formula for the height of a tetrahedron.
blocks.solution:
In a cube of side $s$, choose four vertices no two of which share an edge, for example $(0,0,0)$, $(s,s,0)$, $(s,0,s)$, $(0,s,s)$. Each pair is joined by a diagonal of a face, of length $s\sqrt2$, so these four points form a regular tetrahedron with edge $s\sqrt2$.

The cube minus the tetrahedron consists of four corner pieces. Each is a tetrahedron with three mutually perpendicular edges of length $s$ meeting at a cube vertex: a pyramid with right-triangle base of area $\frac12 s^2$ and height $s$, so of volume $\frac16 s^3$. Therefore the regular tetrahedron has volume $s^3 - 4\cdot\frac16 s^3 = \frac13 s^3$.

With $a = s\sqrt2$, that is $s = \frac{a}{\sqrt2}$, the volume is $\frac13\cdot\frac{a^3}{2\sqrt2} = \frac{a^3}{6\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{12}a^3$.

blocks.title: Half full?
blocks.body: A conical glass, point downwards, is filled with water to half its height. What fraction of the glass's volume is water?
blocks.solution: The water itself forms a cone similar to the glass with scale factor $\frac12$. By the scaling law its volume is $\left(\frac12\right)^3 = \frac18$ of the glass's. A glass filled to half its height holds only one eighth of its capacity; to be half full by volume the water must reach $\left(\frac12\right)^{1/3} \approx 0.79$ of the height.

blocks.body:
- Area scales by $k^2$ and volume by $k^3$, not by $k$. A model at scale $1:50$ has $\frac{1}{2500}$ of the area and $\frac{1}{125000}$ of the volume.
- The sector and arc formulas $\frac12 r^2\theta$ and $r\theta$ need $\theta$ in radians.
- In $\frac13\pi r^2 h$ the height $h$ is perpendicular, not the slant height $l$; the slant height appears in the curved surface area $\pi rl$, and $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$.
- Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas: a $1 \times 9$ and a $5 \times 5$ rectangle both have perimeter 20, but areas 9 and 25.
- Do not mix units: $1\ \text{m}^2 = 10^4\ \text{cm}^2$ and $1\ \text{m}^3 = 10^6\ \text{cm}^3$.

The coordinate geometry of solids is in [[solid-geometry]]. The limits hidden in the circle and sphere arguments are made rigorous by the [[riemann-integral]], and [[multiple-integrals]] compute volumes of regions bounded by any surfaces. The general theory of length, area and volume is [[lebesgue]] measure. Area appears in number theory too: counting lattice points in a large disc is a question about [[floor-functions]] whose answer starts with $\pi r^2$.

1. Show that a sphere has two thirds of the volume, and two thirds of the total surface area, of the smallest cylinder containing it.
2. Two similar bottles have heights 20 cm and 30 cm. The smaller holds 400 ml. How much does the larger hold?
3. Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating $y = \sqrt x$, $0 \le x \le 4$, about the $x$-axis.
4. A square pyramid has all eight edges of length 2. Find its height and volume.
